segments.text: High in the sky, the Sun can look almost white.
But near sunset, it can glow orange or red.
The Sun has not changed. The journey of its light has.
Sunlight contains a broad mixture of visible colors.
Together, they can look white.
Now follow that light into Earth's atmosphere.
Air molecules scatter some light away from its original direction.
Shorter wavelengths, like blue, scatter much more strongly than longer wavelengths, like red.
This is called Rayleigh scattering.
Blue light is redirected, not turned into red light.
Some scattered light reaches us from across the sky. That is why the daytime sky looks blue.
When the Sun is high, its light takes a relatively short path through the atmosphere.
Enough of the color mixture remains for the Sun to appear nearly white.
As the Sun sinks toward the horizon, the path through air grows much longer.
More blue light is scattered out of the direct beam.
The remaining light is richer in reds and oranges.
Listen to the same idea. These tones represent colors; light itself is not making sound.
A short path keeps a fuller mix.
A long path leaves much less of the blue component.
Dust, haze, and clouds can change the exact colors you see.
But the central idea stays the same.
One Sun. A longer path through air. A different mix of light reaching your eyes.
